cards.statement: An enforcing plugin gives a later restrictive NetworkPolicy priority over an earlier broad allowance.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy allowances accumulate, so an existing broad allowance survives a more restrictive policy.
cards.misconception: Newer restrictive policies override older allowances.

cards.statement: With enforcement enabled, a destination's ingress allowance overrides its source Pod's egress denial.
cards.explanation: A Pod connection needs permission at both isolated ends; destination ingress permission leaves source egress restrictions intact.
cards.misconception: Destination ingress permission overrides source egress isolation.

cards.statement: A Pod under enforced default-deny egress needs an allowance to reach the cluster DNS service.
cards.explanation: Default-deny egress blocks DNS traffic; workloads need a permitted path to cluster DNS.

cards.statement: The NetworkPolicy API lets a policy author request logging of the connections a policy blocks.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy has no field for logging blocked or accepted connections; any such visibility comes from network plugin features or other tooling.
cards.misconception: NetworkPolicy can ask the dataplane to log the connections it blocks.

cards.statement: NetworkPolicy ingress isolation permits traffic from the selected Pod's resident node.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy exempts ingress from the Pod's local node, leaving that node outside this isolation boundary.

cards.statement: An enforcing plugin's ICMP filtering under default-deny NetworkPolicy depends on its implementation.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy leaves ICMP handling undefined; plugins may permit or drop it.

cards.statement: NetworkPolicy prescribes immediate closure of established TCP sessions after a policy denies their traffic.
cards.explanation: The network plugin determines whether policy changes affect established connections.
cards.misconception: Policy changes prescribe immediate session termination.

cards.statement: Once a plugin handles a NetworkPolicy, it enforces that Pod's isolation for init containers too.
cards.explanation: Processed NetworkPolicy isolation covers init containers because they share their Pod's network.

cards.statement: The API server waits until the network plugin enforces a new NetworkPolicy before it accepts the object.
cards.explanation: The API server stores a valid NetworkPolicy without waiting for the network plugin; the Kubernetes API exposes no enforcement-readiness signal, and plugin processing can lag behind.
cards.misconception: API acceptance confirms installed network enforcement.

cards.statement: A passing kube-bench assessment can establish the security of an application's software dependencies.
cards.explanation: kube-bench assesses Kubernetes configuration; application dependency vulnerabilities need a separate assessment.
cards.misconception: Passing configuration checks establishes dependency security.

cards.statement: A kube-bench FAIL result can reflect a check execution error rather than a configuration mismatch.
cards.explanation: Read kube-bench's remediation output to distinguish a configuration failure from an error that prevented checking.

cards.statement: A kube-bench WARN result counts the assessed setting as compliant with the benchmark.
cards.explanation: WARN needs further assessment, such as a manual check, before administrators determine compliance.
cards.misconception: WARN is a weaker PASS.

cards.statement: A kube-bench Job scheduled on a worker node skips the master checks because it finds no API server running there.
cards.explanation: kube-bench detects which components run on its host and selects tests from that, so control-plane file checks need the Job scheduled on a control-plane node.

cards.statement: Administrators can identify a compatible CIS Benchmark by matching its number to the Kubernetes minor.
cards.explanation: CIS and Kubernetes use separate version schemes; select a benchmark with documented coverage for the cluster.
cards.misconception: Benchmark numbers track Kubernetes minor versions.

cards.statement: In the standard Ingress TLS model, the controller encrypts its connection to backend Pods.
cards.explanation: Standard Ingress TLS ends at the ingress point; backend transport encryption needs separate controller configuration.
cards.misconception: Ingress TLS encrypts the backend connection.

cards.statement: An Ingress needs an explicit rule host matching a tls hosts entry to serve that route with its TLS certificate.
cards.explanation: TLS does not work on the hostless default rule, because its certificate would have to cover every possible hostname; hosts in the tls section must explicitly match rule hosts.

cards.statement: Ingress controllers that read the same Ingress tls section provide the same set of TLS features.
cards.explanation: The Kubernetes docs note a gap between the TLS features of different ingress controllers; check the chosen controller's documentation for how TLS works there.
cards.misconception: Ingress TLS features are portable across controllers.

cards.statement: An Ingress rule with its host omitted can expose a backend through unintended hostnames.
cards.explanation: A hostless rule routes matching paths regardless of the request hostname, broadening backend exposure.

cards.statement: Kubernetes RBAC on the API server decides whether a Pod can query the cloud instance metadata address 169.254.169.254.
cards.explanation: Pods reach the metadata service over the network, outside the Kubernetes API, so RBAC never sees those requests; the checklist says to restrict or block Pod access to it.
cards.misconception: Kubernetes RBAC covers Pod requests to the cloud metadata API.

cards.statement: A kubelet whose KubeletConfiguration file omits readOnlyPort serves unauthenticated read-only data on port 10255.
cards.explanation: In KubeletConfiguration, readOnlyPort defaults to 0, which disables the unauthenticated read-only service; only an explicit port setting turns it on.
cards.misconception: A config-file kubelet opens the unauthenticated read-only port unless an administrator disables it.

cards.statement: A tenant permitted to create Pods and Services with externalIPs can intercept traffic aimed at those IPs.
cards.explanation: Service externalIPs can redirect traffic from other Pods or nodes, making unrestricted tenant use dangerous.

source.title: Kubernetes security advisory: ExternalIPs traffic interception

cards.statement: kubeadm signs kube-apiserver's etcd client certificate with a different CA than its API serving certificate.
cards.explanation: kubeadm keeps a dedicated etcd CA as the trust root for etcd functions and issues kube-apiserver-etcd-client from it, apart from the kubernetes-ca behind the API serving certificate.

cards.statement: A kubectl sha256sum FAILED result shows that someone tampered with the downloaded kubectl binary.
cards.explanation: FAILED only shows the binary and checksum file disagree; a checksum fetched for a different release, for example after stable.txt changes between downloads, fails the same way.
cards.misconception: A failed checksum check always means the download was tampered with.

source.title: Install and Set Up kubectl on Linux

cards.statement: One signing key serves every pkgs.k8s.io Kubernetes minor-version repository, whatever version appears in its key URL.
cards.explanation: The kubectl install guide says the same signing key is used for all Kubernetes package repositories, so the version in the key download URL can be disregarded.

source.title: Install and Set Up kubectl on Linux

cards.statement: A kubectl.sha256 match from dl.k8s.io gives the same assurance of the publisher's identity as cosign verify-blob.
cards.explanation: A checksum only shows the bytes match the published hash file; cosign verify-blob checks a signature and certificate tied to the Kubernetes release signing identity.
cards.misconception: A matching checksum authenticates who published the binary.

cards.statement: Kubernetes v1.35 documents separate signing identities for downloaded binaries and control-plane images.
cards.explanation: The documented binary and image verification examples trust different release identities; use the identity published for that artifact class.
cards.volatilityNote: Release signer identities belong to a beta artifact-publication process and can change.

cards.statement: Verifying a signed Kubernetes SPDX document also verifies a kubectl binary downloaded separately.
cards.explanation: A signature authenticates its signed artifact; verify the downloaded kubectl binary against its own signature and certificate.
cards.misconception: A release inventory signature verifies separate release binaries.

cards.statement: A namespace-wide Secret list permission can reveal object names while keeping their data hidden.
cards.explanation: Secret list responses include Secret contents, so list access exposes credentials.
cards.misconception: Listing Secrets exposes names while withholding values.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: RBAC confines existing resource wildcard grants to APIs present when administrators create the binding.
cards.explanation: Resource wildcards also grant access to resource types added later.
cards.misconception: Resource wildcards capture a fixed API inventory.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: A CSR creator authorized to approve kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client can obtain another user's API credentials.
cards.explanation: CSR creation plus authority to approve the Kubernetes API client signer can yield a certificate bearing another user's identity.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: Removing a user's RBAC bindings can revoke access conferred by system:masters membership.
cards.explanation: system:masters bypasses RBAC checks, so removing bindings leaves its superuser access intact.
cards.misconception: Binding removal revokes system:masters access.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: Users who control admission webhooks can read matched payloads beyond their own object-read grants.
cards.explanation: Configured webhooks receive matching admission objects, granting their operators visibility beyond ordinary object-read permissions.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: A ServiceAccount's automountServiceAccountToken: false blocks token mounts in Pods that set the field to true.
cards.explanation: When both set the field, the Pod spec takes precedence, so a Pod can re-enable the token mount; enforce the restriction with admission policy.
cards.misconception: The ServiceAccount's automount setting overrides the Pod's.

cards.statement: Privileging a namespace's default ServiceAccount exposes Pods that omit an explicit account.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes assigns such Pods the namespace's default account, extending shared privileges to those workloads.

cards.statement: Deleting a namespace's default ServiceAccount disables default account assignment for future Pods.
cards.explanation: The control plane recreates a deleted default ServiceAccount, so deletion fails to provide a durable assignment control.
cards.misconception: Deleting the default account disables future default assignment.

cards.statement: An offline OIDC validator treats a deleted Pod's bound token as valid until that token expires.
cards.explanation: Offline OIDC validation lacks live object-existence checks; a bound token can remain accepted after its Pod is deleted.

cards.statement: With anonymous access on, a kubelet using Webhook authentication treats credential-free requests as system:anonymous.
cards.explanation: Requests that no configured authenticator rejects fall through to the anonymous authenticator; only disabling anonymous access turns them into 401 responses.

cards.statement: A kubelet configured by command-line flags alone, all at their defaults, checks each request against Kubernetes RBAC.
cards.explanation: The kubelet flag defaults to AlwaysAllow, which allows every request; RBAC applies only in Webhook mode, where the kubelet asks the API server through a SubjectAccessReview.
cards.misconception: Kubelet authorization follows API server RBAC out of the box.

cards.statement: A kubelet with token webhook authentication validates a presented ServiceAccount token through the API server.
cards.explanation: The kubelet sends a TokenReview to its configured API server, so bearer-token identity checks use that server's authentication.

cards.statement: The API server verifies the kubelet's serving certificate on its default HTTPS connection to that kubelet.
cards.explanation: The API server's default kubelet connection skips serving-certificate verification. Configuring a trusted kubelet CA bundle closes this server-identity gap.
cards.misconception: HTTPS automatically verifies the kubelet's server identity.

source.title: Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane

cards.statement: With kubelet Webhook authorization, a caller's get on nodes/proxy permits container command execution.
cards.explanation: Some kubelet command endpoints accept WebSocket GET requests. Their authorization uses get, making nodes/proxy access more powerful than read access.

cards.statement: Kubernetes admission controllers validate container commands sent directly to a kubelet's HTTPS endpoint.
cards.explanation: Commands sent directly to the kubelet bypass Kubernetes admission. Restrict this separate endpoint to preserve the cluster's security boundary.
cards.misconception: API server admission also covers direct kubelet commands.

cards.statement: With authorization disabled, etcd accepts data writes from a client using a trusted health-check certificate.
cards.explanation: Client-certificate authentication alone gives a trusted etcd client broad data access; a certificate's health-check purpose supplies no restriction.

cards.statement: Upstream Kubernetes patch releases, including security fixes, cover the three most recent minor versions.
cards.explanation: The project maintains release branches for the three newest minors, each with about a year of patch support; a cluster on an older minor stops receiving upstream security fixes.

cards.statement: A kubeadm control plane upgrade installs the kubelet patch for a worker-node kubelet vulnerability.
cards.explanation: A kubelet security fix has to reach the affected node's kubelet binary. The control plane upgrade leaves that installation to the operator.
cards.misconception: A control plane upgrade also patches worker kubelet binaries.

cards.statement: kube-controller-manager can give each built-in controller its own ServiceAccount and system:controller role.
cards.explanation: With --use-service-account-credentials each controller gets its own identity and role; without it, every control loop shares the controller manager's single credential.

cards.statement: Running a container as an unprivileged user prevents network protocol kernel module autoload.
cards.explanation: Unprivileged processes can trigger some protocol modules by opening suitable sockets. Remove or block unused modules on Kubernetes nodes.
cards.misconception: An unprivileged container cannot trigger kernel module loading.

cards.statement: Write access to a kubelet's configured static Pod manifests gives a user a path to launch local workloads.
cards.explanation: The kubelet watches its configured manifest directory and starts Pods from added files. Protecting writes to that source protects local workload creation.

cards.statement: A user with a node's container runtime socket access can launch containers outside Kubernetes RBAC.
cards.explanation: The runtime accepts local commands through its socket. Its filesystem access controls protect this route to container creation.

cards.statement: An admission rule blocking a runtime socket's exact path can leave access through a parent hostPath mount.
cards.explanation: A hostPath mount of a directory above the socket still exposes the socket, so policy has to forbid mounts that include it directly or through a parent directory.

cards.statement: A bootstrap token holder can forge cluster-info signatures for another client using the same token.
cards.explanation: Bootstrap discovery uses the token as a shared signing secret. A client that knows it can create a valid discovery signature, so sharing one token across clients weakens this trust boundary.

cards.statement: On a node where the kubelet tolerates swap, missing tmpfs noswap support makes the kubelet refuse to start.
cards.explanation: The kubelet logs a warning that memory-backed volumes such as Secrets might swap to disk, then keeps running; provisioning encrypted swap is the administrator's job.
cards.misconception: The kubelet blocks startup when memory-backed volumes could swap.

cards.statement: kubectl treats an untrusted kubeconfig as inert data when accessing a Kubernetes cluster.
cards.explanation: A crafted kubeconfig can execute malicious code on kubectl's host. Inspect configurations from untrusted sources before use.
cards.misconception: A kubeconfig cannot execute code or expose files on its consumer's host.

source.title: Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files

cards.statement: An admission allowlist confines an untrusted Pod to its approved read-write hostPath directory.
cards.explanation: Directory allowlisting needs read-only hostPath mounts to preserve the intended boundary; an untrusted writer can subvert a writable mount.
cards.misconception: Admission directory allowlisting securely confines read-write hostPath access.

cards.statement: With direct API server-to-kubelet networking, a node firewall blocking that path breaks kubectl logs.
cards.explanation: The API server retrieves Pod logs through the kubelet's HTTPS endpoint. Node firewall rules need to preserve this control-plane path for log requests to succeed.

source.title: Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane

cards.statement: A process under an AppArmor profile in complain mode completes a file write outside the profile's rules.
cards.explanation: Complain mode only reports profile violations and does not block them, so it suits profile development rather than containment; switch to enforce mode before relying on it.

source.title: Linux kernel security constraints for Pods and containers

cards.statement: When its requested Localhost AppArmor profile is missing, kubelet can start a Pod with RuntimeDefault.
cards.explanation: A Pod requesting a Localhost AppArmor profile fails to start when that profile is unavailable on its node. Kubernetes does not substitute RuntimeDefault.
cards.misconception: Kubernetes falls back to RuntimeDefault when a requested local AppArmor profile is unavailable.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

cards.statement: The default scheduler can place an AppArmor-constrained Pod using its inventory of loaded node profiles.
cards.explanation: The scheduler does not track loaded AppArmor profiles. Administrators can use node labels and placement constraints to select nodes prepared for the workload.
cards.misconception: The scheduler discovers which AppArmor profiles each node has loaded.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

cards.statement: A node's /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles file names the container processes attached to each listed profile.
cards.explanation: That file lists loaded profiles and their modes. To see the profile a container's root process runs under, read /proc/1/attr/current inside the container.
cards.misconception: The node's loaded-profile list shows which container uses each profile.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

cards.statement: The seccomp SCMP_ACT_LOG action permits a matching syscall through its filter while recording it.
cards.explanation: SCMP_ACT_LOG records a syscall and permits execution. That action supplies observations for building a restrictive profile.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: With externalTrafficPolicy Cluster, kube-proxy on a node hosting zero of a Service's Pods forwards its NodePort traffic.
cards.explanation: Each node proxies a NodePort Service's port, so every node becomes an entry point; restrict exposure with node firewalls or kube-proxy nodePortAddresses.

cards.statement: The runtime retains a configured seccompProfile when it starts a container with privileged: true.
cards.explanation: Privileged containers run with seccomp Unconfined. An explicit profile in the workload specification does not keep syscall filtering active.
cards.misconception: An explicit seccompProfile remains effective when the container runs privileged.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: Moving a RuntimeDefault seccomp Pod from containerd nodes to CRI-O nodes can change its allowed syscall set.
cards.explanation: RuntimeDefault defers to each node runtime's bundled profile, and runtimes and their releases can ship different syscall lists, so test the workload on every runtime it may run on.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission enforces Baseline in an unlabeled namespace when its AdmissionConfiguration sets no defaults.
cards.explanation: With no namespace labels and no configured defaults, Pod Security Admission applies the Privileged level, so it restricts nothing. Set labels or configuration defaults to enforce a level.
cards.misconception: Pod Security Admission enforces Baseline out of the box.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards by Configuring the Built-in Admission Controller

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission lets a namespace enforce Baseline while using Restricted checks in its warn mode.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission uses independent mode-level labels. Operators can check a stricter target in warn mode while enforcing a compatible level.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission can supply secure field defaults to a Pod before applying a namespace's Restricted policy.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission validates submitted Pods rather than setting security fields. Supply required values in the workload or a separate mutating admission step.
cards.misconception: Pod Security Admission sets secure defaults as part of its validation.

source.title: Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission preserves a namespace's v1.35 checks across upgrades when enforce-version stays v1.35.
cards.explanation: A Pod Security Admission version label fixes a mode's checks to that Kubernetes minor's policy instead of following the latest policy.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission rejects a Deployment whose template violates its namespace's Restricted enforce policy.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission's enforce mode checks Pods created from a Deployment, rather than the Deployment request. Workload templates receive audit and warning checks.
cards.misconception: Enforce mode rejects workload templates at Deployment admission.

cards.statement: A user with unrestricted namespace patch access can weaken that namespace's labeled Pod Security Admission enforcement.
cards.explanation: Changing namespace labels can relax Pod Security Admission's policy level. Reserve namespace update rights for trusted users.

source.title: Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller

cards.statement: In a namespace enforcing Baseline v1.35, Pod Security Admission rejects a nonexempt Pod with a nonempty HTTP probe host.
cards.explanation: The Baseline policy includes the probe host restriction introduced in v1.34. An HTTP probe's host field has to be empty or omitted.

cards.statement: A Linux Pod can pass Restricted admission with Pod and container seccompProfile omitted if its node uses seccompDefault.
cards.explanation: Restricted Pod Security Admission requires an explicit RuntimeDefault or Localhost seccomp profile at Pod or container level. Node runtime defaulting leaves the required API field absent.
cards.misconception: Node seccomp runtime defaults satisfy Restricted admission's explicit-profile requirement.

cards.statement: After a namespace switches to Restricted enforce mode, Pod Security Admission evicts its running violating Pods.
cards.explanation: Changing a namespace's enforce label checks existing Pods and reports violations as warnings. Pod Security Admission leaves those running Pods in place.
cards.misconception: Strengthening an enforce policy evicts existing noncompliant Pods.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels

cards.statement: An admitted Pod exposes its mounted Secret to its creator despite RBAC restrictions on that user's direct Secret reads.
cards.explanation: A Pod creator chooses code that consumes the mounted Secret, exposing its value through workload access rather than direct API reads.

cards.statement: Mounting a needed Secret lets operators avoid granting its Pod's ServiceAccount namespace-wide Secret API read access.
cards.explanation: Secret mounts provide needed values while keeping the Pod's ServiceAccount outside a broader Secret-read permission grant.

cards.statement: Under default Linux container isolation, a compromised sidecar reads a Secret mounted solely into its sibling.
cards.explanation: Secret mounts grant container-specific access. Restrict them to containers that need the credentials.
cards.misconception: Siblings inherit Secret volume access from sharing a Pod.

cards.statement: With Secrets encrypted in etcd, an application's crash-dump logs can still expose Secret environment variables.
cards.explanation: Secret values in environment variables can enter crash dumps and logs after the application receives plaintext.

cards.statement: With several etcd members, TLS on the API server's etcd client connection covers member-to-member replication traffic.
cards.explanation: etcd secures peer traffic with its own peer certificate and key, configured separately from client TLS; without it, data replicated between members travels unprotected.
cards.misconception: Client TLS to etcd protects peer replication too.

cards.statement: With KMS v2 configured, the API server encrypts Secret data locally while a remote KMS protects its key material.
cards.explanation: The API server handles payload encryption with derived DEKs; the external KMS protects key material instead of receiving Secret payloads.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: With KMS v2, revoking the API server's access to the remote KEK immediately blocks reads that use already cached DEKs.
cards.explanation: KMS v2 caches unwrapped DEKs in the clear and keeps decrypting with them indefinitely without calling the KMS, so revoking KEK access does not block reads that use those cached keys.
cards.misconception: Revoking remote KMS access invalidates cached plaintext keys.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: An attacker who compromises a control plane host can extract a locally managed aescbc key that protects Secrets in etcd.
cards.explanation: The local key is stored on the host in the EncryptionConfiguration file, so local encryption protects against an etcd-only compromise but not against a host compromise.

cards.statement: For an API server using a configured KMS v2 plugin, rotating the remote KEK requires restarting that API server.
cards.explanation: The API server detects KMS v2 key rotation through Status polling and keeps running during the change.
cards.misconception: KMS v2 remote-key rotation requires an API server restart.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: With ordinary containers sharing a worker node, namespace separation keeps a container escape inside its tenant.
cards.explanation: Namespaces group API resources and policies; they do not separate a shared node's kernel.
cards.misconception: Namespace boundaries contain host access gained through a container escape.

cards.statement: A tenant's virtual control plane isolates cluster-wide admission webhooks from other tenants' API configurations.
cards.explanation: Separate tenant control planes avoid conflicts over cluster-scoped objects such as admission webhooks, giving tenants independent API policy configuration.

cards.statement: Dedicated tenant nodes prevent lateral movement through Kubernetes credentials exposed on a compromised node.
cards.explanation: An attacker can use node-exposed credentials against shared cluster services to reach other tenants.
cards.misconception: Dedicated worker nodes confine the reach of their exposed Kubernetes credentials.

cards.statement: On one node, two RuntimeClasses with different names give their Pods the same isolation when they share a handler.
cards.explanation: A RuntimeClass's handler names the CRI configuration on the node and its object name only identifies the RuntimeClass, so a sandbox-sounding name adds no isolation when the handler points at an ordinary runtime.

cards.statement: When a RuntimeClass handler is unavailable, kubelet can start its Pod with the node's default runtime handler.
cards.explanation: A Pod fails when its selected RuntimeClass handler is unavailable; kubelet does not substitute the default handler.
cards.misconception: RuntimeClass handler failures silently fall back to the node's default runtime.

cards.statement: With WireGuard encryption enabled, Cilium-managed Pods exchange same-node traffic through an encrypted tunnel.
cards.explanation: Cilium leaves same-node traffic outside its WireGuard tunnel; local host access already exposes the plaintext.
cards.misconception: Cilium WireGuard encryption also tunnels local traffic between Pods on one node.

cards.statement: With Cilium IPsec encryption enabled, a node capture can show decrypted inner traffic alongside encrypted ESP packets.
cards.explanation: The host recirculates decrypted IPsec packets for processing. A capture can include plaintext after decryption alongside outer ESP packets.

cards.statement: In Istio sidecar mode, PERMISSIVE lets server Envoy upgrade a plaintext client's connection to mutual TLS.
cards.explanation: PERMISSIVE accepts plaintext alongside mutual TLS. A client sending plaintext keeps that connection unencrypted.
cards.misconception: PERMISSIVE upgrades directly received plaintext connections rather than accepting plaintext.

cards.statement: In Istio sidecar mode, client Envoy can reject a server's valid mesh certificate for a mismatched HTTP service.
cards.explanation: Istio's client Envoy checks whether the server's ServiceAccount identity is authorized to run the target service. A trusted mesh certificate alone does not establish that association.

cards.statement: Kubernetes recommends ephemeral debug containers as an alternative to packaging debug utilities in production images.
cards.explanation: Keep the production image focused on the application and its dependencies. An ephemeral debug container provides troubleshooting tools separately.

cards.statement: Node OS updates can patch a minimal image's retained libraries through the node's package manager.
cards.explanation: An image packages its application and system libraries separately from the host. Fix a packaged library in a new image and recreate the container from that image.
cards.misconception: Patching a node's operating system also patches libraries packaged inside its container images.

source.title: Containers: Container images and host independence

cards.statement: A validly signed attestation passes cosign verify-attestation even when its predicate fails the supplied CUE policy.
cards.explanation: With --policy, cosign checks the attestation's predicate against CUE or Rego rules and reports validation errors on any violation, even when the signature itself is valid.
cards.misconception: A valid attestation signature is enough for cosign verify-attestation to pass.

cards.statement: Trivy's SPDX relationships show investigators which inventoried packages depend on a suspect library.
cards.explanation: SPDX dependency relationships connect an inventoried library to the packages that need it, helping investigators trace where that dependency enters the image.

source.title: SBOM: Supported packages and SPDX relationships

cards.statement: By default, a Trivy CycloneDX image report is a package inventory that omits vulnerability findings.
cards.explanation: Trivy treats CycloneDX output as an SBOM: --format cyclonedx turns off security scanning by default, and vulnerabilities appear only with --scanners vuln.

cards.statement: An SBOM's valid SPDX structure establishes the package metadata Trivy needs for accurate vulnerability matching.
cards.explanation: Trivy relies on custom SBOM properties for accurate scanning. A valid SPDX document can still omit metadata needed for reliable package identification.
cards.misconception: A valid SBOM format guarantees the metadata quality needed for accurate vulnerability scanning.

source.title: SBOM scanning: External SBOM metadata limitation

cards.statement: By default, Trivy returns a success exit status to CI after an image scan reports vulnerability findings.
cards.explanation: A CI job that treats scanner success as approval can publish an image with findings. Set a failure exit status for the chosen policy and make the pipeline honor it.
cards.volatilityNote: Trivy's default exit-code behavior is a project CLI default that could change across releases.

cards.statement: Shared node-level registry credentials let the kubelet enforce tenant-specific access to private images.
cards.explanation: Pods on a node can access private registries authorized by shared node credentials. Namespace separation does not give those credentials a separate authorization scope for each tenant.
cards.misconception: Shared registry credentials on a node preserve separate image access rights for individual tenants.

cards.statement: An attacker controlling a CI system's OIDC identity can obtain Sigstore certificates under that identity.
cards.explanation: Sigstore can issue certificates to a compromised OIDC identity. Protecting the CI identity remains part of the signing trust boundary.

source.title: Sigstore Threat Model: OIDC account compromise

cards.statement: By default, policy-controller rejects an image in an opted-in namespace when no ClusterImagePolicy pattern matches it.
cards.explanation: Without a no-match-policy setting, policy-controller denies images that match no ClusterImagePolicy, so unlisted registries stay blocked; warn or allow relaxes this.

cards.statement: A registry policy's static pass authority verifies the signer of an image it admits through policy-controller.
cards.explanation: policy-controller's static pass authority accepts matching images without checking their signatures.
cards.misconception: Registry allowance also proves a trusted signer.

cards.statement: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy CEL rule can reject Deployments whose container images use an unapproved registry prefix.
cards.explanation: The v1.35 docs show a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that checks container image prefixes with CEL, so the API server enforces permitted registries without a webhook.

cards.statement: A valid image signature establishes that the workload is safe for production use in a Kubernetes cluster.
cards.explanation: Software safety needs a separate assessment; signature verification does not evaluate the workload's behavior.
cards.misconception: A valid signature proves production safety.

cards.statement: Cosign keyless verification checks an expected certificate identity together with its expected OIDC issuer.
cards.explanation: An authorization policy identifies both the intended signer and the identity provider trusted to authenticate that signer.

cards.statement: Cosign verification confirms the signed digest matches the target image while default claim checks stay on.
cards.explanation: Cosign's claim checks compare the image digest in the signature payload with the image being verified.

cards.statement: In an opted-in namespace, policy-controller automatically pins admitted image tags to resolved digests.
cards.explanation: policy-controller's tag resolution ties deployment to the content evaluated during admission.

cards.statement: During validation, policy-controller admits an image that passes one matching enforce policy and fails another.
cards.explanation: policy-controller combines matching enforcing ClusterImagePolicy resources with AND; admission requires satisfying them.
cards.misconception: Matching image policies are alternatives.

cards.statement: Cosign invalidates a historically valid keyless image signature when its signing certificate expires.
cards.explanation: Cosign uses a trusted timestamp to evaluate certificate validity at signing time, preserving later verification.
cards.misconception: Certificate expiry invalidates historical signatures.

cards.statement: Kubesec flags requested SYS_ADMIN authority even when the manifest sets the container's runAsNonRoot to true.
cards.explanation: Kubesec evaluates the requested capability as a separate risk. A non-root setting does not erase that configuration finding.

source.title: Kubesec: Security risk analysis for Kubernetes resources

cards.statement: Kubesec changes a schema-valid Pod's valid result to false when it finds a critical security risk.
cards.explanation: A Kubesec result can show valid=true alongside critical security findings. Resource validity and risk findings are separate results.
cards.misconception: Critical risk findings also invalidate the resource validation result.

cards.statement: An ignore-check annotation in a workload's own manifest can make KubeLinter skip that check for the object.
cards.explanation: KubeLinter honors ignore-check.kube-linter.io/<check> and kube-linter.io/ignore-all annotations, so a clean result can reflect an author's exemption rather than a compliant setting.

cards.statement: KubeLinter's remediation output can rewrite the scanned Pod manifest to apply its recommended security settings.
cards.explanation: KubeLinter reports recommended changes. An operator or a separate automation step applies the remediation to the manifest.
cards.misconception: KubeLinter applies the manifest fixes described by its remediation messages.

cards.statement: By default, a Trivy image scan also reports secrets found in image files alongside vulnerable packages.
cards.explanation: Trivy enables vulnerability and secret scanning by default for container images, so credentials left in image files appear in results; misconfiguration and license scanning stay off unless enabled.

cards.statement: A vendor package's older upstream version can coexist with a backported fix that Trivy recognizes.
cards.explanation: Trivy uses OS-vendor advisories for vendor packages; backported fixes can change vulnerability status while retaining an older upstream version.

source.title: Trivy: Vulnerability Scanning: Handling Software Installed via OS Packages

cards.statement: Trivy's default severity selection can replace its selected vendor's lower rating with NVD's higher rating.
cards.explanation: Trivy prefers the selected vendor's severity because it reflects distribution-specific build and configuration choices.
cards.misconception: Trivy defaults to the highest severity supplied by NVD or the vendor.

cards.statement: Trivy's OS-package scan covers a self-compiled library copied into an image beside vendor-managed packages.
cards.explanation: OS-package detection relies on vendor-managed packages. A copied self-compiled library sits outside that package coverage.
cards.misconception: OS-package scanning also covers software copied into the image outside the vendor's package system.

cards.statement: Trivy's comprehensive mode resolves the actual installed version from a dependency range in requirements.txt.
cards.explanation: Trivy uses the range's minimum for vulnerability matching. That estimate can differ from the version an application actually installs.
cards.misconception: Comprehensive range scanning determines the exact version installed by the application.

cards.statement: With a shell-spawn rule enabled, Falco's alert leaves containment to a separately configured response integration.
cards.explanation: Falco detects the rule match and emits an alert. A response integration takes any containment action.

cards.statement: On an instrumented Linux node, Falco observes supported host-process events alongside container events by default.
cards.explanation: Falco's syscall monitoring spans the shared host kernel, so host processes also fall within its observation scope.

source.title: Falco: Missing Fields in Falco Logs

cards.statement: With cluster audit logging enabled, Falco's syscall source receives API server audit records automatically.
cards.explanation: The k8s_audit source needs its event-source plugin and an audit-event feed; syscall monitoring does not supply these records.
cards.misconception: Enabling cluster audit logs automatically adds their records to Falco's syscall event source.

cards.statement: Putting container.id in a Falco rule's output restricts that rule's matches to events from container processes.
cards.explanation: Falco's condition selects event scope. Printing container.id adds context to an alert rather than filtering host events.
cards.misconception: A container field in an alert output also filters the events eligible to trigger that rule.

source.title: Falco: Basic Elements of Falco Rules

cards.statement: Dropped syscall events can distort Falco's process and file metadata, weakening rules that use that cached state.
cards.explanation: Falco builds its internal process and file view from events; capture loss can leave that view incomplete or inaccurate.

source.title: Actions For Dropped System Call Events

cards.statement: When two Falco rules match a syscall event, their priorities determine which rule Falco evaluates first.
cards.explanation: Rule priority describes alert severity. Falco's rule evaluation order follows definition and loading order.
cards.misconception: Falco treats priority as rule precedence rather than alert severity.

cards.statement: A Falco exception for one actor-target pair leaves that actor eligible for alerts on other matching targets.
cards.explanation: The paired exception suppresses that actor-target combination. Activity by that actor at other matching targets remains eligible for alerts.

cards.statement: With its container plugin configured, Falco can alert before a runtime lookup supplies the container's image metadata.
cards.explanation: Container enrichment depends on lookup timing; a missing image field alone does not establish that an event came from a host process.

cards.statement: With syscall and Kubernetes audit sources enabled, a Falco rule can join their events into a combined attack sequence.
cards.explanation: Falco partitions rules by event source. Correlating syscall and audit events needs a separate analysis layer.
cards.misconception: Enabling multiple sources makes cross-source event correlation available inside a Falco rule.

cards.statement: Falco rule outputs can name a container shell's grandparent and earlier ancestor processes alongside its parent.
cards.explanation: Ancestor fields such as proc.aname[2] and proc.apid[2] take an index, so an alert can show the chain from a shell back to the process that started the session.

source.title: Falco: Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs

cards.statement: With Falco's container plugin providing Pod UIDs, investigators distinguish replacement Pods sharing a name.
cards.explanation: Match the captured Kubernetes Pod UID to the investigated Pod object. A reused namespace/name may refer to a replacement Pod.

source.title: Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs

cards.statement: A container's readOnlyRootFilesystem setting blocks writes through its separately mounted writable emptyDir.
cards.explanation: readOnlyRootFilesystem protects the container's root filesystem. A separately mounted writable emptyDir remains a place to alter files.
cards.misconception: Making the container root filesystem read-only also freezes separately mounted writable volumes.

cards.statement: Falco's incubating Change thread namespace rule excludes setns calls made by runc during container setup.
cards.explanation: setns often runs while a container is created, so the rule's condition excludes runc, containerd and other known tools; it alerts on setns by an unexpected program, such as an nsenter escape attempt.

cards.statement: With supported overlayfs detection, investigators treat Falco's upper-layer executable flag as runtime drift evidence.
cards.explanation: An executable in the overlayfs upper layer indicates container drift. Legitimate debugging or setup also produces this evidence.

cards.statement: During an investigation, Falco's recorded process name reliably locates the executable file on disk.
cards.explanation: A process can have a custom name. Investigators use executable-path evidence to locate the launched file on disk.
cards.misconception: The process name recorded in a syscall event reliably identifies the executable's path.

source.title: Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs

cards.statement: For a kubectl exec session, Falco's syscall user field identifies the API user who starts the interactive shell.
cards.explanation: Falco records the process's operating-system user. Attribute kubectl exec callers by correlating with API audit evidence.
cards.misconception: A syscall event's process user reveals the Kubernetes API identity responsible for starting that process.

source.title: Falco: Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs

cards.statement: When open flags are O_WRONLY, a successful open event in Falco proves that the process changed the file's contents.
cards.explanation: A successful O_WRONLY open grants write access to an existing file; it does not establish a completed write to its contents.
cards.misconception: Opening an existing file for write access is evidence that a process completed a content modification.

source.title: Falco: Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs

cards.statement: Falco's upper-layer executable flag also marks a binary that an attacker drops into a mounted emptyDir volume.
cards.explanation: proc.is_exe_upper_layer reports executables in the overlayfs upper layer. An emptyDir is node storage mounted into the Pod, so binaries dropped there fall outside that flag.
cards.misconception: The upper-layer flag catches every binary written after the container starts.

source.title: Falco: Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs

cards.statement: With a backend configured, kube-apiserver can record Secret bodies when matching None precedes matching RequestResponse.
cards.explanation: Audit policy uses the first matching rule. A preceding None match suppresses the event.
cards.misconception: A later detailed audit rule overrides an earlier exclusion.

cards.statement: With a configured backend, Request-level auditing records the response body of a successful Secret read.
cards.explanation: Request captures request bodies; RequestResponse includes responses. Metadata excludes both bodies.
cards.misconception: Request auditing captures the object returned by a read.

cards.statement: With a backend and Metadata policy configured, kube-apiserver can emit ResponseStarted for a watch request.
cards.explanation: ResponseStarted marks the beginning of a streaming response, before completion.

cards.statement: An audit policy rule selecting pods also selects requests to pods/exec through that parent-resource match.
cards.explanation: An audit rule naming pods excludes subresources; select pods/exec or a suitable wildcard to capture exec requests.
cards.misconception: Selecting the parent resource also selects its subresources.

cards.statement: For a configured audit webhook, kube-apiserver requires an audit policy file to generate request records.
cards.explanation: The API server leaves its audit webhook inactive when its policy evaluator is absent.

cards.statement: When a policy and its matching rule both list omitStages, kube-apiserver omits the union of the two lists.
cards.explanation: Policy-wide and rule-level omitStages combine, so a rule cannot re-enable a stage that the policy omits; stages in neither list still produce events.

cards.statement: A replacement kube-apiserver Pod inherits audit files stored in the previous Pod's writable container layer.
cards.explanation: Persist audit files outside the API server container's ephemeral filesystem.
cards.misconception: Container-layer audit files survive replacement of the Pod.

cards.statement: When its audit batch buffer overflows, kube-apiserver can retain excess events by waiting for buffer space.
cards.explanation: An overflowing batch buffer drops audit events, leaving gaps in the evidence.
cards.misconception: Audit batching applies backpressure to preserve excess events when its buffer fills.

cards.statement: With blocking-strict auditing, kube-apiserver fails a request when auditing fails at RequestReceived.
cards.explanation: A RequestReceived logging failure in blocking-strict mode makes audit availability affect API availability.
